title: Saving Water at Home
summary: Where Saudi Arabia gets its fresh water, why that water is costly and limited, and simple ways every family can save water at home.
poll: Children can make a real difference in saving water.

versions.title: Save Water at Home
versions.text:
Turn on the tap. Out comes clean water! It seems so easy. But in Saudi Arabia, it is hard to get.

The land has no big rivers. It has no lakes. It does not rain much. So where does it all come from?

A lot comes from the sea. But the sea is too salty to drink. Big plants take the salt out. This costs a lot. It uses lots of power, too.

Some is deep in the ground. It took a long, long time to fill up. It will not fill up fast.

So we must save water. You can help at home!

Shut the tap when you brush your teeth. Take a short shower. Does a tap drip? Tell an adult. A leak can waste a lot in a year.

Run the wash when it is full. Give your plants a drink when the sun is low. Then less of it dries up.

Each drop counts. Small steps add up!

versions.title: Saving Water at Home
versions.text:
When you turn on the tap, clean water pours out. It seems simple. But in Saudi Arabia, getting fresh water to millions of people is a huge job.

Saudi Arabia has no rivers that flow all year. It has no large lakes, and rain is rare in most areas. So where does the water come from?

Much of it comes from the sea. Sea water is far too salty to drink, so huge plants along the coast remove the salt. This process is called desalination. Saudi Arabia makes more of this water than any other country. But the process costs a lot of money and uses a great deal of energy.

The rest comes mostly from groundwater. It is stored in rock deep below the ground. Much of it collected thousands of years ago, when the climate was wetter. Today it refills very slowly, so it could run out.

That is why it is important to conserve water. Each family can help at home.

Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. A running tap can waste several liters every minute. Take short showers instead of filling a bath. If a tap drips, tell an adult. A small leak can waste thousands of liters in a year.

Run the washing machine and dishwasher only when they are full. Water plants in the early morning or evening. Then less water is lost to evaporation in the hot sun. Water-saving devices on taps and showers can also help.

Every drop counts, and small steps from millions of people add up to a lot.

When you turn on the tap, clean water pours out instantly, and it seems effortless. In Saudi Arabia, however, supplying fresh water to millions of people is an enormous and expensive challenge.

The country has no permanent rivers or large lakes, and rainfall is infrequent across most regions, so its water must come from other sources.

Much of it comes from the sea. Because sea water is far too salty to drink, enormous facilities along the coast remove the salt through a process called desalination, and Saudi Arabia produces more desalinated water than any other country. However, desalination is expensive and consumes a tremendous amount of energy.

Most of the remaining water is groundwater, which is stored in an aquifer, an underground layer of rock that holds water like a sponge. Much of this water accumulated thousands of years ago, when the climate was considerably wetter, and today it is replenished so slowly that it is not truly renewable.

For these reasons, reducing water consumption is essential, and every family can contribute at home.

Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth, since a running tap can waste several liters every minute, and take short showers instead of filling a bath. If a tap drips, inform an adult immediately, because even a small leak can waste thousands of liters annually.

Outdoors, families can wash cars with a bucket instead of a running hose, and gardeners can install drip irrigation, which delivers water slowly through small tubes directly to the roots of plants.

Every drop counts, and small actions taken by millions of people combine to make water use more sustainable.

When you turn on the tap, clean water pours out instantly, and the process seems effortless; in Saudi Arabia, however, supplying fresh water to millions of people is an enormous and extraordinarily expensive undertaking.

The country has no permanent rivers or large lakes, and precipitation is infrequent across most regions, so its water must originate from alternative sources, each of which is either expensive or fundamentally limited.

Much of it comes from the sea: because seawater is far too salty to drink, enormous facilities along the coast remove the salt through a process called desalination, and Saudi Arabia produces more desalinated water than any other country. Nevertheless, desalination is expensive and consumes a tremendous quantity of energy.

Most of the remaining water is groundwater, which is stored in an aquifer, an underground layer of porous rock that holds water like a sponge. Much of this water accumulated thousands of years ago, when the climate was considerably wetter, and today it is replenished so slowly that it is not genuinely renewable.

For these reasons, reducing household water consumption is essential, and every family can contribute meaningfully by modifying several everyday routines.

Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth, since a running tap can waste several liters every minute, and take short showers instead of filling a bath. If a tap drips, inform an adult immediately, because even a small leak can waste thousands of liters annually.

Operate the washing machine and dishwasher exclusively when they are completely full, which is considerably more efficient than running several partial loads. Water plants in the early morning or evening, so that less moisture is lost to evaporation in the intense heat. versions.title: Saving Water at Home
versions.text:
When a household tap is opened, clean water emerges instantaneously, creating an impression of effortless abundance; in Saudi Arabia, however, supplying fresh water reliably to millions of residents constitutes an extraordinarily complex and prohibitively expensive undertaking that few people fully appreciate.

The Kingdom possesses no permanent rivers and no substantial natural lakes, while precipitation remains sporadic across the overwhelming majority of its territory, meaning its water supply must originate from alternative sources, each burdened by its own significant limitations or expense.

A substantial proportion derives from the sea: because seawater remains far too saline for human consumption, enormous coastal facilities extract dissolved salt through an energy-intensive process called desalination, and Saudi Arabia produces more desalinated water than any other nation worldwide. Nevertheless, this process remains prohibitively expensive and consumes staggering quantities of energy in the process.

Most remaining water originates as groundwater, stored within an aquifer, an underground stratum of porous rock that retains water much as a sponge retains moisture. The overwhelming majority of this water accumulated millennia ago, during a considerably wetter climatic period, and because contemporary replenishment occurs so gradually, this resource cannot genuinely be classified as renewable.

Given these fundamental constraints, reducing household water consumption becomes absolutely essential, and every family can contribute meaningfully by modifying several routine daily habits.

Turning off the tap while brushing teeth prevents considerable waste, since a continuously running tap squanders several liters every minute, while brief showers conserve substantially more water than filling an entire bathtub. Any dripping tap should be reported immediately to an adult, since even a seemingly minor leak can waste thousands of liters annually without detection.

Operating washing machines and dishwashers exclusively when completely full proves considerably more efficient than running multiple partial loads sequentially. Watering plants during early morning or evening hours minimizes moisture lost to evaporation during intense daytime heat, while water-saving attachments fitted to taps and showers can further restrict flow rates; the national Qatrah program, whose name means "drop" in Arabic, actively encourages citizens and residents alike to adopt precisely these responsible conservation habits.

Beyond the household, families can wash vehicles using a bucket rather than a continuously running hose, while gardeners can install drip irrigation systems, which deliver water gradually through narrow, perforated tubing directly toward plant roots, where it is genuinely needed and where considerably less evaporates before absorption occurs.

Ultimately, every conserved drop matters significantly, and the cumulative effect of countless small individual actions, multiplied across millions of households, renders the nation's overall water consumption considerably more sustainable for generations yet to come.

versions.title: Saving Water at Home
versions.text:
When a household tap is opened, clean water emerges instantaneously and effortlessly, creating a deceptively simple impression of limitless abundance; in Saudi Arabia, however, reliably supplying fresh water to millions of residents constitutes an extraordinarily complex, resource-intensive, and prohibitively expensive logistical undertaking that few consumers fully appreciate or comprehend.

The Kingdom possesses no permanent rivers and no substantial natural lakes, while precipitation remains sporadic and unpredictable across the overwhelming majority of its vast territory, meaning its entire water supply must originate from alternative sources, each burdened by its own significant limitations, scarcity, or considerable expense.

A substantial proportion of this supply derives from the sea: because seawater remains far too saline for direct human consumption, enormous coastal facilities extract dissolved salt through an extraordinarily energy-intensive industrial process called desalination, and Saudi Arabia consequently produces more desalinated water than any other nation worldwide. Nevertheless, this essential process remains prohibitively expensive to operate and consumes genuinely staggering quantities of energy throughout the extraction process.

Most of the remaining supply originates as groundwater, retained within an aquifer, an underground geological stratum of porous rock that holds water much as a sponge retains absorbed moisture. The overwhelming majority of this ancient water accumulated many millennia ago, during a considerably wetter climatic era, and because contemporary natural replenishment occurs so gradually and imperceptibly, this finite resource cannot genuinely be classified as renewable in any practical sense.

Given these fundamental geological and economic constraints, reducing household water consumption becomes an absolute civic necessity, and every individual family can contribute meaningfully toward this goal by modifying several routine daily habits.

Turning off the tap deliberately while brushing teeth prevents considerable unnecessary waste, since a continuously running tap squanders several liters every single minute, while deliberately brief showers conserve substantially more water than filling an entire bathtub repeatedly. Any dripping tap discovered at home should be reported immediately to a responsible adult, since even a seemingly negligible leak can waste many thousands of liters annually without anyone noticing the cumulative loss.

Operating washing machines and dishwashers exclusively when they are genuinely full proves considerably more resource-efficient than repeatedly running multiple partial loads throughout the week. Watering plants specifically during early morning or evening hours minimizes moisture needlessly lost to evaporation during periods of intense daytime heat, while specialized water-saving attachments fitted onto taps and showerheads can further restrict unnecessary flow rates; the national Qatrah initiative, whose name translates as "drop" in Arabic, actively and persistently encourages citizens and residents alike to adopt precisely these responsible, sustainable conservation habits.

Beyond the immediate household, families can wash vehicles using a simple bucket rather than relying on a continuously running hose, while dedicated gardeners can install drip irrigation systems, which deliver water gradually and precisely through narrow, perforated tubing directly toward plant roots, exactly where moisture is genuinely required and where considerably less evaporates before meaningful absorption occurs.

Ultimately, every individually conserved drop matters significantly within this larger equation, and the cumulative effect of countless small, deliberate actions, multiplied consistently across millions of households nationwide, renders the entire nation's overall water consumption considerably more sustainable for generations of residents yet to come.

MID.modelAnswer: Saving water is especially important in Saudi Arabia because the country has no rivers that flow all year and very little rain. Much of its water comes from desalination, which removes salt from sea water but costs a lot of energy, and the rest comes from groundwater that collected underground thousands of years ago and refills very slowly. Because these sources are limited and expensive, every family needs to conserve water so it does not run out.

keyWords.definition: a layer of rock or soil under the ground that holds water
keyWords.example: The village well draws water from a deep aquifer.

keyWords.definition: able to be replaced naturally as fast as it is used
keyWords.example: Sunlight is a renewable source of energy.

keyWords.definition: the amount of something that is used
keyWords.example: Our electricity consumption is higher in summer because of the air conditioner.

keyWords.definition: doing a job well without wasting time, energy, or materials
keyWords.example: An efficient car can travel far on a small amount of fuel.

keyWords.definition: able to continue for a long time without harming the environment
keyWords.example: The farm uses sustainable methods so the soil stays healthy.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Its water sources are costly or limited, so households must use less.
Desalination has completely solved all of Saudi Arabia's water problems forever.
Groundwater in Saudi Arabia refills quickly after rain.
Only farmers need to save water.
questions.why: The article explains the expense of desalination and the slow refilling of aquifers, then urges families to cut water use.

wrong.C: The article says it is replenished very slowly.

questions.stem: According to the article, why is the groundwater not truly renewable?
options: It is polluted by factories.
It is replenished far more slowly than it is used.
It is too deep to reach.
It turns into salt water.
questions.why: The article says the water accumulated thousands of years ago and is replenished so slowly that it is not truly renewable.

wrong.C: People do pump it; depth is not the issue given.
wrong.D: The article does not say this.

questions.stem: What does the name of the national program Qatrah mean?
options: River
Rain
Drop
Ocean
questions.why: The article says Qatrah means "drop" in Arabic.

wrong.A: This is not the meaning given.
wrong.B: This is not the meaning given.
wrong.D: This is not the meaning given.

questions.stem: In the article, the word efficient most nearly means…
options: using resources without waste
very loud
extremely expensive
finished quickly but done very badly
questions.why: Running full loads instead of partial ones uses water without waste, which is what efficient means.

wrong.D: Efficient means doing a job well.

questions.stem: How do desalination and groundwater compare as water sources?
options: Both are unlimited and cheap.
Both come from rivers.
Groundwater needs much more energy to produce than desalination does.
Desalination uses much energy; groundwater refills slowly.
questions.why: The article describes desalination as expensive and energy-intensive, and groundwater as slowly replenished.

wrong.A: Neither is described as unlimited or cheap.
wrong.B: Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers.
wrong.C: The article stresses desalination's energy use.

questions.stem: What is the effect of using drip irrigation in a garden?
options: Plants receive water at their roots, and less is wasted.
Plants receive salt water from the sea.
The garden needs more water than before.
The hose runs continuously.
questions.why: The article says drip irrigation delivers water directly to the roots through small tubes.

wrong.B: Drip irrigation does not use sea water.
wrong.C: Its purpose is to use less water.
wrong.D: A running hose is what the article says to avoid.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin by describing water pouring easily from a tap?
options: To show readers how easy it is to install a brand-new tap in the kitchen
To contrast how easy water seems with how hard it is to supply
To explain how desalination works
To describe a leak
questions.why: The opening shows that water seems effortless, then reveals that supplying it is an enormous challenge.

wrong.D: Leaks come later in the article.

questions.stem: What can you infer about the purpose of the Qatrah program?
options: To build new rivers across the country
To sell more washing machines
To persuade people to reduce water consumption at home
To stop desalination completely
questions.why: The program encourages people to adopt water-saving habits like those in the article.

wrong.B: The article mentions machines only to use them fully.
wrong.D: The article does not say desalination will stop.

HIGH.prompt: Imagine you are designing a water-saving campaign for your school. Which three habits from the article would you promote, and why would they make water use more sustainable?
checklist: I chose three habits from the article.
I explained why each one saves water.
I connected my ideas to Saudi Arabia's water sources.
HIGH.modelAnswer: For my school's water-saving campaign, I would promote three habits from the article. First, turning off the tap while brushing teeth saves water because a running tap wastes several liters every minute. Second, watering plants in the early morning or evening reduces evaporation in the hot sun, so less water is lost before it reaches the roots. Third, using efficient water-saving devices on taps and showers reduces the amount of water that flows out without anyone changing their habits. These three habits matter because Saudi Arabia relies on expensive desalinated water and slow-renewing groundwater, so using water more sustainably protects a limited resource.
